messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 44

**Patient Vignette: Dr. M.**

Dr. M. is a 62-year-old Latin American surgeon, a man who has spent the last thirty-five years of his life with a scalpel in his hand, his reputation built on steady, unshakeable precision. He presents for the first time at the urging of his wife, Maria, who has watched him change over the past eight months. He sits forward in the chair, hands clasped, his posture still that of a man accustomed to command, but his eyes are tired.

The event occurred on a Tuesday. He was driving home after a sixteen-hour shift, a complex hepatic resection that had gone perfectly. He remembers the rain, the way the streetlights smeared across his windshield. He remembers the flash of headlights, the squeal of tires that wasn’t his own. A pickup truck ran a red light at sixty miles per hour. Dr. M. doesn’t remember the impact. He remembers waking up in his own car, the airbag deflated, the smell of gasoline and hot metal filling the cabin. He was pinned, the steering wheel crushed against his sternum. He remembers the firefighter’s face, young and scared, telling him to stay still. He remembers thinking, with absolute clarity, *I am going to die in this car. I have three children. I have a wife. I am going to die in this car.*

He did not die. He suffered three broken ribs, a fractured clavicle, and a deep laceration on his right forearm—his operating arm. The physical wounds healed. The scar is a thin, white line now. But the surgeon who returned to the OR six weeks later is not the same man.

The operating room, once his sanctuary of control, has become a crucible of dread. The first time he scrubbed in again, his hands began to tremble. He attributed it to weakness, to disuse. But the tremor did not stop. It worsened when the overhead lights were adjusted, casting a particular shadow. Now, every case is a battle. The smell of Betadine, the hiss of the ventilator, the specific *click* of a clamp—each sound is a trigger. He has started to assign a junior resident to stand by the door, just in case he needs to "step out." He has never actually left a table, but the thought is a constant, humming terror. He finds himself rehearsing escape routes during a cholecystectomy, calculating how long it would take to get the patient closed if he had to run. He is terrified that his hands will fail him, that he will freeze mid-procedure, and a patient will bleed out because of his cowardice.

The hypervigilance has bled into every corner of his life. He cannot drive. He sold his car and takes a medical transport service to the hospital, sitting in the back, eyes closed, counting his breaths. He avoids the highway. Any sudden sound—a dropped tray in the hospital cafeteria, a car backfiring—sends his heart into a gallop. He has become irritable with the nurses, snapping at them for what he knows is nothing. He apologized to a scrub nurse yesterday for yelling at her about a missing suture, and then he went into the locker room and cried. He has not told anyone about the crying.

At night, he sleeps in the guest room. Maria finds him there most mornings, sitting on the edge of the bed, still dressed in the clothes he wore the day before. He tells her he doesn't want to disturb her rest. The truth is he is afraid of the dreams. They are not the accident itself. They are fragments: the smell of gasoline, the sound of his own breathing under the mask of the firefighter, the feeling of the steering wheel against his ribs. He wakes up gasping, his hand reaching for a scalpel that isn't there.

He used to be a man of few words, but now he is silent. At family dinners, he stares at his plate. He has stopped playing with his grandchildren, afraid that if he picks up the baby, his hands will shake, and he will drop her. He feels a profound, corrosive shame. He has saved thousands of lives. He has held a still-beating heart in his palm. And now, he is undone by a car accident. He tells me he is not a victim. He is a surgeon. Surgeons do not have flashbacks. Surgeons do not jump at the sound of a closing door. But he does, and he cannot make it stop.
